g.text: Reinforcement learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving
mathematical reasoning in large language models.
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Reinforcement learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models.

g.text: DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) demonstrated that RL can incentivize
sophisticated reasoning behaviors, while Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) introduced an efficient approach that eliminates
g.title: N2 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) demonstrated that RL can incentivize sophisticated reasoning behaviors, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) introduced an efficient approach that eliminates the need for a separate value function by using group-relative advantage estimation.

g.text: Building on these advances, iGRPO (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) extends GRPO
with a two-stage draft-conditioned training procedure: the model first
generates multiple draft solutions, selects the best draft based on reward,
g.title: N3 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Building on these advances, iGRPO (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) extends GRPO with a two-stage draft-conditioned training procedure: the model first generates multiple draft solutions, selects the best draft based on reward, and then trains on refinements conditioned on this selected draft.

g.text: This approach achieves strong gains on math reasoning benchmarks under
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) This approach achieves strong gains on math reasoning benchmarks under matched compute budgets.

g.text: Question: draft quality vs two-stage structure
However, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does iGRPO's benefit
come from conditioning on high-quality drafts, or from the two-stage
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does iGRPO's benefit come from conditioning on high-quality drafts, or from the two-stage structure itself?

g.text: The original iGRPO method selects the highest-reward draft for conditioning,
but it is unclear whether this quality-based selection is necessary.
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) The original iGRPO method selects the highest-reward draft for conditioning, but it is unclear whether this quality-based selection is necessary.

g.text: Two competing hypotheses about draft role
If the benefit primarily comes from exposing the model to an in-context
"attempt" (regardless of correctness), then even a low-quality draft should
provide similar gains. Conversely, if draft quality is essential,
g.title: N7 [Limitation] (cites=0) If the benefit primarily comes from exposing the model to an in-context "attempt" (regardless of correctness), then even a low-quality draft should provide similar gains. Conversely, if draft quality is essential, conditioning on incorrect drafts should substantially reduce performance.

g.text: To answer this question, we design a controlled ablation study with three
conditions: (A) GRPO baseline without draft conditioning, (B) iGRPO with
best-of-N draft selection (the original method), and (C) iGRPO with
g.title: N8 [Method] (cites=0) To answer this question, we design a controlled ablation study with three conditions: (A) GRPO baseline without draft conditioning, (B) iGRPO with best-of-N draft selection (the original method), and (C) iGRPO with worst-of-formatted draft selection (our ablation variant that intentionally selects low-quality but well-formatted drafts).

g.text: All conditions use matched compute, enabling a clean comparison of draft
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) All conditions use matched compute, enabling a clean comparison of draft selection strategies.

g.text: Our results reveal a surprising finding: conditioning on worst-of-formatted
drafts not only recovers but exceeds the performance of best-of-N selection.
g.title: N10 [Result] (cites=0) Our results reveal a surprising finding: conditioning on worst-of-formatted drafts not only recovers but exceeds the performance of best-of-N selection.

g.text: iGRPO-worst achieves 64.37% macro-average accuracy compared to iGRPO-best's
61.94% (+2.43 pp), with a recovery ratio of 1.34 (95% CI: [1.21, 1.47]) on
g.title: N11 [Result] (cites=0) iGRPO-worst achieves 64.37% macro-average accuracy compared to iGRPO-best's 61.94% (+2.43 pp), with a recovery ratio of 1.34 (95% CI: [1.21, 1.47]) on MATH500.

g.text: Analysis reveals that worst-of-formatted selection produces 50% more
gradient-active training groups, potentially explaining its superior
g.title: N12 [Result] (cites=0) Analysis reveals that worst-of-formatted selection produces 50% more gradient-active training groups, potentially explaining its superior performance.

g.text: Finding 1: clean ablation isolates draft quality
(1) we design a clean ablation study that isolates the role of
draft quality in iGRPO by comparing best-of-N vs
worst-of-formatted draft selection under matched compute;
g.title: C1 [Contribution: Finding 1] (cites=0) (1) we design a clean ablation study that isolates the role of draft quality in iGRPO by comparing best-of-N vs worst-of-formatted draft selection under matched compute;
